items.stem: A developer wants to skip the application tier and let the browser send SQL straight to the database. What is the main problem?

options.text: The database password would have to sit in code on the user's device.
options.feedback: The browser runs on a device the user controls. Anything stored there can be read, so the middle tier must hold the password.

options.text: Browsers are too slow to send SQL queries across the internet to a database.
options.feedback: Speed is not the issue. The issue is who holds the credentials and who decides which queries are allowed.

options.text: A database can only accept connections from a single computer at a time.
options.feedback: Databases accept many connections. The application tier is needed for security and rules, not for connection limits.

options.text: Without the middle tier, the page could no longer show HTML to the user.
options.feedback: The browser would still show HTML. The change would remove the one tier that enforces permissions.

items.stem: A student edits the student number in the address bar and sees another student's grades. Which tier should have refused the request?

options.text: The application tier, which checks who is logged in before querying.
options.feedback: The application tier knows who is logged in and decides which rows that person may see.

options.text: The browser, because it already knows which student is logged in.
options.feedback: The browser runs on the user's device and the user can change anything in it. It cannot be trusted to enforce rules.

options.text: The database, because it holds the grades and knows who owns them.
options.feedback: The database answers any query it is given by a trusted caller. It does not know which student is logged in.

options.text: None of them, because anything in the address bar is public.
options.feedback: The address bar is visible, but access to the data still has to be checked on the server.

items.stem: The database has just returned two rows. What happens next, before the browser receives anything?

options.text: The application tier turns the rows into objects, then JSON.
options.feedback: Rows go back to the application tier, which builds objects and converts them to JSON text for the response.

options.text: The database sends the rows directly to the browser.
options.feedback: The database only talks to the application tier. The browser never connects to it.

options.text: The browser turns the rows into page elements.
options.feedback: That happens later, after the browser has received the JSON response.

options.text: The rows are sent to the browser as SQL text.
options.feedback: SQL goes from the application tier to the database. The browser receives JSON.

items.stem: A student opens the enlistment page on a phone. Which tier is running on the phone itself?

options.text: The browser tier, which shows the page.
options.feedback: The browser runs on the user's own device. The other two tiers run on servers you manage.

options.text: The application tier, because it handles the student's request.
options.feedback: The application tier runs on your server. The phone only sends the request and receives the response.

options.text: The database tier, because the grades are saved there.
options.feedback: The database runs on your server or its own machine. The phone never connects to it.

options.text: All three tiers, because the page needs all of them.
options.feedback: The page needs all three tiers, but only the browser tier runs on the phone.
